title: {actor} leans too far left
text: {actor} leans into the kiss and keeps leaning. {other} is now holding a very sincere diagonal.

title: {actor} loses the staircase
text: Climbing the stairs, {actor} tilts one degree a step. At the top, the staircase and {actor} disagree about which way is up.

title: {actor} drifts into the wings
text: {actor} has leaned so gradually that the speech is now being delivered, with great feeling, to a curtain.

title: The waltz becomes a knot
text: The waltz begins well. By the third bar {actor}'s strings have found {other}'s, and the dance continues as one ambitious knot.

title: {actor} fills the watering can
text: {actor} weeps so sincerely that the watering can overflows. The front row is invited to consider their shoes.

title: {actor} cries at the wedding
text: {actor} cries at the vows, which is reasonable, and again at the buffet, which is not.

title: The watering can waters the scenery
text: {actor} has quietly been watering the {object} with the can. It was never going to bloom, but the effort is noted.

title: The letter becomes porridge
text: {actor} is handed a letter, reads it aloud, weeps into it, and the letter becomes soup. {other} improvises the will.

title: {actor} apologises to the victim
text: {actor} raises the dagger, lowers it, and begins an apology that outlasts the plot. {other} is asked to wait.

title: {actor} checks the duel is comfortable
text: Mid-duel, {actor} stops to ask if {other} would like a sit-down. {other} says 'Quite, thank you.' The duel resumes, warmer.

title: Poison, with an apology
text: {actor} pours the poison, then offers {other} tea instead, 'in case it is a bad day for it'.

title: {actor} apologises to {town}
text: {actor} apologises to the whole of {town} for the villainy ahead, and promises to keep it brief.

title: The chandelier is looking at {actor}
text: The chandelier sways. {actor} stops mid-menace and says, in a small voice, 'It is looking at me.' It is, a little.

title: {actor} dives for cover
text: Thunder shakes the chandelier. {actor} dives for cover and finds {other}, who is not furniture but is, for now, helping.

title: A villain behind {other}
text: {actor} delivers the entire villain monologue from behind {other}, in case of falling things.

title: The aisle takes a detour
text: At the wedding, {actor} will not walk under the chandelier. The aisle is now three metres wider and passes the bar.

title: {actor} meets the spotlight
text: {actor} steps into the light for the first time and waits for the prompt. The prompt waits for {actor}. A courteous standoff.

title: {actor} thanks the audience, personally
text: A laugh arrives. {actor}, who has never been laughed at, nor with, stops the play to thank the house individually.

title: {actor} knows every exit
text: {actor} knows where every exit is, having watched from the wings for years, and uses all of them. Politely.

title: Every line, in the wrong order
text: {actor} knows every line of every part and delivers them in the order they come to mind, which is not the play's.

title: {actor} says all the parts
text: {actor} recites every part under the scene, half a second early. {other} has nothing left to say and says so, ahead of time.

title: A helpful whisper, loudly
text: {actor} whispers {other}'s line to {other} a beat early, helpfully, in front of the entire house.

title: A very good speech, wrong play
text: {actor} knows the villain's speech very well. It is the wedding. It is a very good speech.

title: {actor} fights both sides
text: {actor} knows the choreography for both duellists and performs all of it alone, at speed, losing to {actor} with great dignity.

title: {actor} plays every part
text: {actor} plays both halves of the love scene, changing wigs at speed. Somewhere in the middle, {actor} marries the wrong wig.

title: {actor} eats the wedding cake
text: Mrs. Gasket sends on a wedding cake. {actor} was told it was a prop, and has been testing the theory ever since.

title: {actor} eats the evidence
text: A letter containing the secret is handed to {actor}, who eats it. The secret is now safe, and also digested.

title: Only one guest is eating
text: At the feast, {actor} is the only guest still eating and, to be fair, the only guest still in character.

title: The treasure was chocolate
text: The treasure turns out to be chocolate coins. {actor} discovers this slowly, then entirely. The plot develops a gap.

title: {actor} exits into the cupboard
text: {actor} exits with great authority through the door marked CUPBOARD. The scene continues. So does the sound of mops.

title: {actor} exits into the audience
text: {actor} exits through the wrong door, which opens onto the auditorium. A seat is found. The scene is watched from row C.

title: Five entrances, no exits
text: {actor} makes five entrances in a row, each through a door never meant to be one. Nobody has the heart to stop it.

title: {actor} finds the trapdoor
text: Looking for the door, {actor} finds the trapdoor, which is more of a hole in a bad mood. The scene continues from below.

title: {actor} steps in front of the moon
text: {actor} steps in front of the paper moon for a solo nobody asked for. The moon is lowered, quietly. The moon remembers.

title: The moon and {actor} exchange a look
text: {actor} dances in front of the paper moon. The moon dips to reclaim the light. They exchange a look that will last years.

title: {actor} turns the moon around
text: {actor} delivers the soliloquy to the paper moon, then turns the moon to face the wall so it cannot steal the ending.

title: A coronation, with the moon
text: {actor} takes the crown, the spotlight and the moon (in that order) and leaves the scene somewhere to the left of them all.

title: {actor} sneezes out the candles
text: A ball mask arrives with a feather. {actor} regards the feather; the feather regards {actor}. The sneeze snuffs every candle in the {place}.

title: A sneeze in B flat
text: A feather of unknown origin drifts by. {actor} sneezes; a goose, offended, honks. They reach an understanding in B flat.

title: The disguise blows away
text: {actor} is disguised as a bird, which is the problem. By the second sneeze the mask is in the dress circle, and so is the plot.

title: A coronation, horizontally
text: A crown arrives with a plume. {actor} sneezes eleven times, faints, and is crowned lying down. It is felt to be a modern reading.

title: It is not Act Two
text: It is Act One. {actor} delivers the Act Two reconciliation with total confidence. {other} has not yet been wronged.

title: The letter has not been written
text: {actor} reveals the secret of the letter. The letter has not been written yet. {other} writes it hastily during the gasp.

title: The jury is a chair
text: In the version {actor} knows, the jury is a chair. {actor} addresses it for three minutes. The chair, to its credit, listens.

title: {actor} exits for the interval
text: {actor} exits for the interval that comes in Act Two. It is forty minutes away. {actor} is found in the {place}, eating an orange.

title: {actor} dies for six minutes
text: {actor} is struck down and dies for six minutes, in three languages. {other} checks the programme: 'dies briefly'.

title: A death down every stair
text: {actor} falls down the entire staircase, one step at a time, with a small salute at each landing.

title: {actor} dies ahead of the poison
text: {actor} dies a full minute before the poison could possibly work. The poison, embarrassed, goes and sits down.

title: A ghost with a second act
text: {actor} dies, is covered by Mrs. Gasket's sheet, remembers a line, rises as a ghost and delivers it. The ghost gets the applause.

title: The curtain falls on a long death
text: Clipboard calls the curtain on {actor}'s death. It sticks at knee height. The death continues underneath, visible from the shins.

title: Nothing rhymes with orange
text: {actor} reaches for a rhyme for 'orange', finds none, and delivers the line as a long and dignified silence.

title: The whole stage scans
text: Everyone on stage is now speaking in couplets. {actor} started it. {other} is losing, and knows it.

title: A rhyming death
text: Dying, {actor} insists on a rhyme for 'expire'. The death takes four minutes. {other} offers 'higher' and is thanked.

title: My heart sings like a cart
text: 'My heart, my heart, it sings like a cart,' says {actor}. {other} nods slowly, as if it were the finest poetry.

title: The secret is out in row F
text: {actor} stage-whispers the secret the whole plot hangs on. Row F confirms: 'We heard.'

title: Exit, pursued by a bear
text: {actor} whispers the stage directions for the back row: '(exits, pursued by a bear)'. A bear is sourced.

title: Sorry, in a whisper, to everyone
text: {actor} apologises to the Prompter in a whisper the whole house can hear. Then apologises for the whisper.

title: {actor} whispers 'I love you'
text: {actor} whispers 'I love you' to {other}. It is heard in the next town. {other} replies at the same volume, which is only fair.

title: {actor} meets the chair
text: {actor} has met the chair. It is the one. The scene waits while {actor} recites a sonnet about its legs.

title: A mutual gaze
text: Mrs. Gasket wheels on a mirror. {actor} sees it, and the gaze is mutual. The mirror is, as ever, an excellent listener.

title: {actor} proposes to the crown
text: Mrs. Gasket brings the crown on a cushion. {actor} proposes to it. The crown accepts, being in no position to do otherwise.

title: {actor} will not give it back
text: {actor} has fallen for the {object} and will not hand it over, not even to {other}, not even when the plot needs it.

title: {actor} adopts the umbrellas
text: {actor} falls for the umbrella stand, adopts all eleven umbrellas, and introduces each by name to anyone who will stand still.

title: {actor} winds down mid-speech
text: Halfway through the big speech, {actor} winds down. The last syllable lasts a full minute and ends like a gate.

title: Mrs. Gasket brings the key
text: Mrs. Gasket arrives with the key and, with eight hands, winds the wrong thing. {actor} performs the scene backwards, politely.

title: {actor} has fainted (wound down)
text: {actor} winds down at the height of the tragedy. The cast, assuming a faint, fan {actor} with a programme.

title: The verdict never comes
text: {actor} winds down while pointing at the guilty party. Everyone holds the pose until Clipboard calls cue 31.

title: The corpse is laughing
text: {actor} dies beautifully, then begins to giggle. The funeral continues around a corpse that is visibly enjoying it.

title: The corpse gets up to be the ghost
text: Mrs. Gasket covers the late {actor} with a sheet. {actor} sits up too early. The ghost is now a corpse in a sheet.

title: The deceased waves at row D
text: {actor}, deceased, waves at someone in row D. Row D waves back. The funeral is now a reunion.

title: {actor} is in a different play
text: In the middle of the drama, {actor} shouts 'It's behind you!' at {other}. Nobody is behind anyone. Everyone looks.

title: A duel in a drawing room
text: {actor} draws a sword in a play with no swords. Mrs. Gasket supplies an umbrella with a nod. They duel, politely.

title: A wig from another play
text: {actor} enters in the wig from a different play and addresses {other} as someone who has been dead since Act Two.

title: The play that must not be named
text: {actor} cannot name the Scottish play, calls it 'that one with the hands', spins three times and spits. A candle goes out, in sympathy.

title: The guest who must not be named
text: Seeing the ghost at the feast, {actor} says 'that fellow' and refuses to say who. The ghost is offended and sits at the end.

title: Thunder, and a very careful word
text: Thunder. {actor} wants to say the name, wants to very much, and instead holds a six-second silence with great courage.

title: {actor} bows in Act One
text: A single cough is heard. {actor} mistakes it for applause, bows, and leaves. The play is not over. {other} says so, at length.

title: {actor} bows to a stuck curtain
text: The curtain sticks half-way. {actor} bows to it, to the house, and to the curtain again, and holds the pose until released.

title: A corpse takes a bow
text: {actor} dies and, hearing a sniffle, rises to bow, remembers, and lies down again with enormous tact.

title: A kiss blown to row C
text: {actor} blows a kiss to a cousin in row C. Row C sends one back. {other} stands in the crossfire, looking slightly kissed.

title: {actor} asks for the snacks
text: In the middle of the speech, {actor} asks the front row to pass the snacks. The front row, to its credit, does.

title: A borrowed umbrella
text: {actor} borrows an umbrella from the third row for the storm scene. It is returned, with a note, at the end.

title: {actor} thanks the Prompter
text: The prompt arrives. 'Thank you!' says {actor}, to the whole house, and then, a beat late, the line.

title: A line, loyally mis-heard
text: {actor} mishears the prompt and, loyally, delivers 'The tea is snowing, my lord.' {other} accepts this.

title: {actor} argues with the Prompter
text: {actor} disagrees with the prompt, in a whisper. The Prompter whispers back. {actor} apologises, with feeling, to the whole box.

title: {actor} takes a walk in row E
text: During the quiet scene, {actor} drifts off the stage and sits down in someone's coat. The scene continues, slightly emptier.

title: A candle goes for a walk
text: {actor} sleepwalks the length of the {place}, carrying a candle, and is applauded at the far end like a small lighthouse.

title: {actor} sleepwalks down the banister
text: {actor} sleepwalks down the banister and reaches the bottom asleep and in excellent time. Row A calls it the best bit.

title: {actor} ties a bow
text: {actor} walks through {actor}'s own strings, then the scenery, then {other}. The result is a knot with a pulse.

title: A figure of eight, accidentally
text: During the dance, {actor} and {other} find they are one set of strings. The dance continues, as a figure of eight.

title: Strung up on the stairs
text: {actor} reaches the top of the stairs and discovers the stairs have kept hold of one string. A pause follows, then a tug.

title: {actor} flees by the trapdoor
text: {actor} flees the swaying chandelier by the nearest exit, which is the trapdoor. The chandelier, satisfied, stops swinging.

title: {actor} opens an umbrella indoors
text: In the ballroom, {actor} opens an umbrella against the chandelier. Indoors. Several superstitions leave the room.

title: {actor} eats the wig
text: Mrs. Gasket hands {actor} a spare wig. It is a prop. It is also, now, lunch.

title: {actor} apologises to the cake
text: A wedding cake arrives. {actor} apologises to it before cutting it. The cake accepts. The cutting is postponed until further notice.

title: The watering can meets the candle
text: A candle is lit for the sad bit. {actor} weeps on it. The candle hisses. A small silence follows, then applause for the candle.

title: {actor} haunts the moon
text: In the ghost scene, {actor} borrows a sheet and haunts the moon directly. The moon does not blink. It has no lids.

title: A mask in love
text: Mrs. Gasket hands {actor} a mask. {actor} falls for it at once. The mask takes the news well, as masks do, and does not change expression.

title: The curtain stalls, in rhyme
text: 'The curtain falls!' says {actor}. It does not. 'The curtain stalls!' tries {actor}, which scans, and is accurate.

title: A cure for the lean
text: To stop the lean, Mrs. Gasket ties {actor} to {other}. The lean is cured. The scene now travels as one.
